title: Twelve names (Mark 3:7–19)
hook: he calls twelve to be with him and to be sent, including the one who'll betray him

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man in the middle of a watching room, their hardness grieving him, told to reach. Your line was stretch out your hand. Did you do the awkward good thing? Day one hundred sixty-eight. Twenty-four weeks.

By now the crowds are enormous. Mark lists where they come from: Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, the desert country to the south, across the Jordan, even the coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon. So many that Jesus asks for a small boat to stand by, in case he's crushed on the shore. And right then, at the height of it, he walks away from the crowd. He goes up into the hills and calls a handful of people by name. Not the biggest donors or the best speakers. Fishermen. A tax collector. A man who'll one day hand him over. Today's word is what they became.
screen: `CROWDS FROM EVERYWHERE.` → `A BOAT STANDING BY.` → `UP INTO THE HILLS.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the old King James Bible: "And he ordained twelve, that they should be with him, and that he might send them forth to preach." Two jobs, in that order. First, to be with him. Then, to be sent. The Greek word for one who is sent is apostolos, and it gives us apostle. An apostle isn't first a manager or a speaker. It's someone sent, and in Mark, someone who has been with Jesus before they're sent anywhere. Why twelve? Israel had twelve tribes, and some readers hear Jesus gathering a renewed people around him, one for each tribe. Then Mark reads out the names, like a roll call. Simon, whom he names Peter, which means rock. James and John, the sons of Zebedee, whom he nicknames "Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder." Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, another James, Thaddaeus, another Simon, called the Zealot or the Canaanite. And the last name on the list comes with a note nobody would put in a founding document: "Judas Iscariot, which also betrayed him." Mark tells you before you've grown attached. Jesus chose him anyway, and kept him close to the end. That closes a week in Mark. A man with leprosy, touched. Four friends through a roof. Levi's table. New wine. Grain on the sabbath. A withered hand. And now twelve names, first called to be with him.
screen: `TO BE WITH HIM, THEN TO BE SENT.` · `APOSTOLOS — ONE WHO IS SENT.` · `TWELVE, LIKE THE TRIBES.` · `A ROLL CALL THAT ENDS WITH JUDAS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: twelve people who shaped you. Settle, and breathe. Let names come, one at a time, like a roll call. A parent or grandparent. A teacher. A friend from a hard year. Someone who hurt you and taught you something anyway. Someone whose name you've forgotten but whose kindness you haven't. Don't rank them. Just count them in. If you get stuck, wait; one more will come. If you pray, you can thank God for each name. After the bell, write them down. The bell holds the time.
Apostle. From the Greek apostolos, one who is sent. In Mark, called first to be with him, then sent.
Your line: first, to be with him. Today, before you're sent into anything, a meeting, a task, a hard talk, take a minute to just be with whoever or whatever you rely on. Day one hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Christians honor the twelve apostles, and many churches keep feast days for them through the year; Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches describe their bishops as standing in succession from the apostles, while many Protestant churches speak of being apostolic by holding to the apostles' teaching.

original.note: Greek: one who is sent, from apostellō, to send away. It gives English apostle.

trapdoor: what you thought: an apostle is a very senior saint.
what it means: someone sent. in Mark, the twelve are called first to be with Jesus, and only then sent out.
what a scholar hears: apostolos, a sent one. and the list's lesser names vary a little between the gospels, like Thaddaeus and Judas son of James.
